1318-the-twin-hells-a-thrilling-narrativ:
John N. Reynolds, who served sixteen months in the Kansas penitentiary and time in Missouri's, tells what he saw inside: the cells, the stripes, the labor, and the cruelty of the keepers. His narrative names names and spares no detail of the twin hells of his title.

Reynolds writes as a witness and a reformer, urging readers to end the abuses he suffered. The book is raw, angry, and firsthand. It stands as a document of American prison life in the nineteenth century, and it still shocks with its plain testimony.
1333-robert-f-murray-author-of-the-scarl:
Andrew Lang, the Scots man of letters, writes a memoir of Robert F. Murray, a young St. Andrews poet who died at twenty-nine, and gathers his poems beside it. Murray's verse, touched by the university town and by illness, is light, learned, and melancholy.

Lang's memoir gives the poems their human frame: a brief life, a circle of friends, and a promise cut short. The volume preserves a minor poet who might else be lost. It suits readers who like Victorian verse and the friendship of letters. Lang's memoir preserves a young poet who might else be lost.
19728-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Nut growers in the northern United States formed an association to share craft knowledge. Its reports record proceedings, papers, and member lists. One surviving page lists pomologists from the Department of Agriculture in Washington. Names like Professor C. P. Close and Walter Van Fleet appear among them. Van Fleet was a noted plant breeder of the era.

Northern nut growing faced cold winters that southern growers escaped. Chestnuts, walnuts, and hickories needed hardy strains and patient testing. Association reports spread results that no single farm could gather. They list who grew what, and where. For farm historians, such lists are gold. They show American horticulture organizing itself, name by name.
19859-a-flat-iron-for-a-farthing-or-some:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote A Flat Iron for a Farthing, passages in the life of an only son. When children clamor for a story, the narrator's wife sends them to him. Tell them how you bought a flat iron for a farthing, she says. He is glad to tell it for three reasons. It is about himself, someone dear, and his own childhood. The tale unfolds as family storytelling.

Ewing was among the finest Victorian writers for children. Her only son narrates with humor and exact memory. A farthing's purchase becomes an epic of childhood economy. Grown readers find real feeling under the comedy. The book influenced later masters of children's fiction. It deserves its classic standing.
20200-christmas-a-happy-time-a-tale-calc:
Christmas: A Happy Time is a tale made for the amusement of young readers. Harriet warns that some hoped-for guests will never come at last. She reminds the others not to open the gate outside. Papa and mamma have both forbidden it, she says with care.

The children shiver in a sharp, cutting wind by that gate. Harriet urges a run round the garden to get warm again. Mamma has begged them not to stand still in such cold. Young readers get a crisp Christmas scene of waiting, hope, and home rules.
20221-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Northern Nut Growers Association reports record yearly meetings of growers and experts. This volume lists members from Nebraska to Ohio and beyond. William Caha of Wahoo and Ward M. Canaday of Toledo appear. Arthur S. Colby of the University of Illinois is also listed.

Such rolls show a wide, keen network behind American nut growing. Reports held talks, elections, and notes on trees and yields as well. Their value now lies in names, places, and dated facts. Readers tracing farm history or family names may find gold here. Growers shared seed, grafts, and hard-won lessons through these yearly gatherings.
20532-love-among-the-chickens-a-story-of:
P. G. Wodehouse published Love Among the Chickens in 1908, subtitled a story of the haps and mishaps on an English chicken farm. The narrator, Jeremy Garnet, is dragged down to Devon by his friend Ukridge. Ukridge plans to make a fortune raising chickens, a subject he knows nothing about.

Garnet reports the scheme's collapse with dry alarm. It is highly improbable, he says, that Ukridge will ever grow old if he repeats his last night's performance. The book mixes farm chaos with a love affair, in the comic style that soon made Wodehouse famous.
20851-character-sketches-of-romance-fict:
Mark Tapley, jolly through every hardship in Martin Chuzzlewit, stars in one sketch here. Dickens's man finds no credit in cheer when life runs smooth. Fever, fraud, and loss in Eden test his creed to the full.

Character Sketches of Romance, Fiction, and the Drama gathers famed figures in short accounts. E. B. Brewer's Reader's Handbook stands behind this vast, handy set. Volume three runs through plays, poems, and novels in alphabetical order. Readers once kept such sets by the desk to place a name or trace a tale in seconds.
20903-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Connecticut names lead the roll in the Northern Nut Growers Association report. Tree experts, doctors, and growers from Stamford to Hartford fill the list. Their meeting papers treat the nuts that thrive in northern soils.

Chestnut, walnut, hickory, and filbert culture fills reports like this one in full detail. Growers swap notes on blight, grafts, soil, and yields by state. The group pushed nut trees as farm crops and shade plantings alike. These proceedings keep the craft of a niche farming world, exact and earnest, for growers and tree lovers to mine.
20915-field-s-chromatography-or-treatise:
Fresh hues on the walls of Theban tombs prove how old the science of colour runs. Field's Chromatography, a treatise on colours and pigments, opens with that deep past. Royal tomb paintings stayed so fresh, it says, as to need no repair.

George Field spent his life on pigments that would not fade or turn. Artists' colours, their making, and their faults fill his famed guide. Later editors rewrote and updated it for new generations of painters. The book stands as a bridge of craft, where chemistry serves art in the studio, colour by tested colour.
20938-stops-or-how-to-punctuate-a-practi:
Commas do too much work, charges Paul Allardyce in Stops, or How to Punctuate. Their vague use, he says, truly harms English style in our time. A firmer system for the old marks would pay at once, he argues.

Allardyce sets out each stop's right work in a practical handbook for writers. Comma, colon, dash, and full stop each get rules and cases. Students and clerks of the pen stood to gain most from its order. The book shows an age that prized clear prose taking its smallest tools with full gravity, mark by mark.
21190-expositions-of-holy-scripture-seco:
Alexander Maclaren, the great Manchester preacher, expounds six New Testament letters in this volume of his Expositions of Holy Scripture. It covers the end of Second Corinthians, Galatians, and Philippians in full, then Colossians, Thessalonians, and First Timothy. Each sermon takes a short text and opens it up.

Titles like Hope and Holiness, Rich Yet Poor, and Strength in Weakness show Maclaren's method. He takes a verse, gives a clear outline, and applies it closely to daily Christian life. He answers the charge that professing Christians often ignore common morality. These printed sermons let readers far from his pulpit study his preaching week by week.
21516-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Growers of nut trees report their results in the Northern Nut Growers Association's printed proceedings. The reports carry the findings of each writer alone, not the backing of the group. A note warns that spray laws and advice may have changed since the papers were written.

Pages treat named kinds of nut trees, grafting, planting, and yields by district. A photo shows a Detroit grower standing under a fine tree, thanks to Gilbert Becker of Michigan. Members swap what worked in one soil and season, with no promise it will work elsewhere. For orchard keepers in cold states, the volume is a trove of trials.
21620-the-myth-of-hiawatha-and-other-ora:
Henry R. Schoolcraft gathers Indigenous tales in The Myth of Hiawatha, published at Philadelphia in 1856. He took the legends from the storytelling circle of the native wigwams. The book is dedicated to Longfellow, whose poem Hiawatha had just drawn on the same store.

Schoolcraft claims the tales show their tellers as they truly are. They reveal what the people believe, hope, fear, wish for, and worship. He argues they place Indigenous character in a wholly new light. As agent and scholar, Schoolcraft spent years among the Ojibwe and others, and his set remains a key, if dated, record.
21829-a-treatise-on-domestic-economy-for:
Running a home is a serious science in Catharine E. Beecher's Treatise on Domestic Economy, first issued in the 1840s for young ladies at home and school. Beecher blames poor health, poor servants, and faulty training for the wives whose strength failed in their first married years. Her book answers with method: health, order, and skill applied to every room of the house.

Chapters teach the care of health, food, children, servants, and the house itself, with engravings to guide the eye. Beecher dedicated the work to American mothers. It became one of the most used housekeeping books of its century. Modern readers find in it both practical lore and a clear window on women's work in 1845.
22094-travels-in-the-great-desert-of-sah:
James Richardson, an English traveller sent to open trade with the Sahara, crossed the great desert in 1845 and 1846. His Travels in the Great Desert of Sahara reports the journey from Tripoli toward the Sudan. Richardson apologises in his preface for the delayed map and commercial reports. The routes he surveyed were meant to guide British trade into the African interior.

He describes wells, caravans, Tuareg and Arab tribes, slavery, and the price of goods. The desert itself, its heat, sand, and thirst, dominates every chapter. Richardson later died on a second, grander expedition. His travels remain a basic source for the Sahara as Europeans first mapped it.
22200-recollections-with-photogravure-po:
David Christie Murray, a popular Victorian novelist, published his Recollections late in his career. The volume carries his portrait in photogravure and a preface of addresses. Murray begins with his birth on the thirteenth of April, which his mother called the unlucky day of the fool's month. He jokes that the phrase proved rich in prophetic wisdom about his life.

From a Birmingham childhood he rose through journalism to the London literary world. The Recollections roam over editors, actors, publishers, and the making of novels. Murray writes easily, with a professional's store of anecdote. His memoir is a useful, genial witness to the book trade of the late nineteenth century.
22238-charles-carleton-coffin-war-corres:
Charles Carleton Coffin was a Civil War correspondent, traveller, and author of boys' histories. This biography, published in 1898 near the end of his life, adds statesman to his titles. Its introduction says Coffin had a face that helped one believe in God. His whole life, the writer claims, was an evidence of Christianity, and he was an organiser of happiness who never sought riches.

Coffin reported Bull Run and a dozen other battles for Boston papers. Later his histories taught two generations of American boys their country's story. This life, written in warm admiration, records the reputation he left: the genial war correspondent who made history read like a story.
22260-bell-s-cathedrals-the-abbey-church:
H. J. L. J. Massé wrote this guide to Tewkesbury Abbey for Bell's Cathedral series. The little books in that series put a scholarly guide into a tourist's pocket. Massé thanks the owners of the Registrum Theokusburiae, the abbey's own register, for lending it for months. He also borrows plates on Saxon churches from the Archaeological Institute's journal, with leave.

Tewkesbury's great Norman tower and its tombs of princes fill the chapters. Massé traces the abbey from its founding through the Dissolution, when the townspeople bought their church to save it. The guide mixes architecture, history, and practical visiting notes. It is a model of the Edwardian church handbook.
22312-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
Growers who raised nut trees formed their own association and printed its proceedings. The Northern Nut Growers Association report records one such meeting. Its pages list members and officers by state and town.

The roll runs from Connecticut and Florida to Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio. Names appear from Panama's Canal Zone as well as Virginia and New York. That spread shows a young industry organizing itself across the country. Inside, readers find the working record of people trading knowledge on nut growing. It preserves names, places, and concerns of early American nut culture that would else be lost.
22400-fox-s-book-of-martyrs-or-a-history:
Fox's Book of Martyrs records the lives, sufferings, and deaths of Christian martyrs. John Foxe's great work stood in English homes beside the Bible for centuries. This edition carries his history of persecution onward.

Its preface argues that persecution is no one creed's vice. Intolerant Jew and bigoted pagan show the same spirit, it says. So do the nominal Christian, the infidel, and the atheist. The urge to force belief is called an inherent vice of fallen nature. Men try to restrain hated opinions by physical pressure. They use the same pressure to spread favored ones. The accounts that follow test that claim in blood.
22460-new-york-times-current-history-the:
The New York Times Current History gathered war news into monthly volumes. Volume two, number five, covers the European War in early 1915. Its pages reprint official notices and reports as they arrived.

On February 4, the German Admiralty proclaimed a war zone. Every enemy merchant ship found around Great Britain would be destroyed. It would not always be possible, Germany warned, to save crews. Passengers, too, would face dangers that could not be averted. That chilling notice marked a turn toward submarine warfare without mercy. Readers today get the war as Americans first read it. It is history in the raw, before outcomes were known.
22471-the-fair-play-settlers-of-the-west:
George D. Wolf studied the Fair Play settlers of the West Branch Valley. Their years, 1769 to 1784, frame his study of frontier ethnography. These settlers governed themselves beyond Pennsylvania's official reach and law.

Wolf calls their story worth telling for one clear reason. It might offer insight into democracy's development on the frontier. His account is an ethnography of how these settlers lived and ruled. He warns it is not meant to typify all frontiers. It is simply an illustration, and he hopes a useful one. Readers get a close case study in self-government. Settlers made law where no law had been provided for them.
22589-jubilation-u-s-a:
Jubilation, U.S.A. is a science fiction story about alien visitors arriving in a very ordinary America. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. In the sample scene, two aliens halt on a road as a wheezing pre-war Chevy chokes its way toward them.

The visitors step into a gully beside the road, ready to run for their ship if the welcome turns hostile. They expect a friendly reception, but they are not sure of their figures. That mix of cosmic travel and small-town caution gives the story its dry comic tone. It belongs to the magazine tradition that played first contact for gentle satire rather than terror. Readers of classic short science fiction will enjoy its deadpan setup.
22721-northern-nut-growers-association-r:
The Northern Nut Growers Association Report of the Proceedings is a conference record from the society that promoted nut growing in northern North America. The catalog record names no editor and gives no year. Papers, discussions, and membership lists make up the volume, as in the association's other reports.

The surviving sample is a roll of members and contacts, state by state: Alabama, Alberta, British Columbia, California, Connecticut, and on through Manitoba, Mexico, and the New England states. Names like Dr. Colt in California and A. Hale in Alberta mark a network of growers swapping varieties and results. Proceedings of this kind carried the practical science of a niche crop. Orchard historians can trace from them how northern nut culture spread.
22831-as-a-chinaman-saw-us-passages-from:
America gets reviewed by a visitor in As a Chinaman Saw Us, a set of letters home from a Chinese traveler. He writes with dry care. The great powers, he notes, believe they are still evolving toward perfection, while Americans assure him the United States has already arrived. Criticizing such a finished nation, he jokes, takes real nerve.

That polite irony runs through the letters. Customs, manners, politics, and national pride all pass before a calm outsider's eye, and his praise often carries a sting. The book belongs to a small shelf of works that reversed the usual travel gaze of the period. It still reads freshly because its main tool, understatement, has not dated at all.
359-good-stories-for-great-holidays-arra:
Frances Jenkins Olcott gathers one hundred and twenty tales for seventeen holidays in this storyteller's volume. New Year, Lincoln's birthday, Valentine's Day, Halloween, and Christmas each get their own set. Tales come grave, gay, funny, or eerie, and many are kept in near-original form for reading aloud.

Olcott notes where a tale is cut short or reshaped for telling, and an index sorts pieces by reading level. Myths, legends, and true stories sit side by side. The book serves parents, teachers, and tellers who want a apt tale for each feast day of the year.
3833-australian-legendary-tales-folk-lor:
K Langloh Parker collected these tales from the Noongahburrah people and set them down as told to children, with an introduction by Andrew Lang. The contents list a whole bestiary of dream time figures. Dinewan the emu and Goomblegubbon the bustard lead the round, with Bahloo the moon, Gooloo the magpie, Weedah the mocking bird, and Meamei the seven sisters behind them. The Borah of Byamee closes the round with sacred law.

One tale follows mother Bunbundoolooey, a pigeon, carrying her crawling child in a netted goolay while she hunts grubs under wattle trees. Parker keeps the tellers' voices close, with native words left in place. Young readers and students of folklore will find a gentle and vivid book, best read aloud, tale by tale.
3892-memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-be:
Lewis Goldsmith presents these secret letters from a gentleman at Paris to a nobleman in London on Napoleon's court at Saint Cloud. The writer, said to be Stewarton, a friend of Josephine in her happier days, gives lives of nearly all Napoleon's ministers and generals, with anecdotes of Napoleon, Talleyrand, and Fouche. The publisher promises particulars found in no other book, including the mysterious disappearance of those who incurred Napoleon's displeasure.

A salon scene shows the new court's strange mixture, with princesses and ci-devant duchesses conversing beside a contractor once a lackey, a duke once a porter, and legislators of every rank. Old nobles and new valets share the same rooms. Readers who like Napoleonic gossip will find a vivid and partisan guide to an upstart court learning old manners.
3893-memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-be:
Lewis Goldsmith's second volume of Saint Cloud letters follows Bonaparte's reach for the German imperial diadem. Austria, Brandenburg, Bavaria, and Baden are cajoled by turns into believing his exclusive support. The writer, tracing a labyrinth of folly and wickedness, meanness and greatness, argues that Bonaparte aims to add Germany's sceptre to the crowns of France and Italy. Electors who refuse to attend him at Mentz must send ambassadors to compliment him instead.

The Pope's arrival forms the second theme, with Sacred College debates long and violent, settled only by four millions of livres spread among cardinals named in a long list. Readers who like Napoleonic intrigue will find a letter book where crowns, tiaras, and bribes change hands in the same paragraph.
3894-memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-be:
Lewis Goldsmith's third volume of Saint Cloud letters writes from Paris in August 1805, praising the king and queen of Naples for grandeur of soul amid a revolutionary volcano. Disturbed at home and defeated abroad, the Sicilian majesties yield territory only to necessity, never to cowardice. Their minister Chevalier Acton, son of an Irish physician settled at Besancon and Leghorn, earns both royal trust and revolutionary hatred.

A darker passage prices the court itself. A minister names his sum for a place, a chamberlain charges for protection, a princess wants a necklace for her interest, and a lady in waiting demands a diamond on promotion day. Secretaries, clerks, cashiers, and messengers all take their fixed price. Readers who like Napoleonic Europe will find a letter book of praise for Naples and contempt for venality.
3895-memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-be:
Lewis Goldsmith's fourth volume of Saint Cloud letters reports Napoleon's cold reception at Milan in August 1805. A brigade of police agents, drilled for years to applaud, goes ahead as his advanced guard, yet the Milanese stay passive or mutinous. Napoleon blames foreign emissaries from envious courts, especially England and Russia, and suspects even Austria of swaying her former Lombard subjects against his solemnity.

The volume then turns to the machinery of rule, with commissions whose weekly imprisonments without cause and transportations without trial show their advantages, and a press whose books prove its liberality. Lenoir Laroche, once an advocate more given to politics than clients, heads one commission. Readers who like the empire's police state will find a bitter and detailed witness.
3896-memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-be:
Lewis Goldsmith's fifth volume of Saint Cloud letters watches Napoleon at the height of his Italian triumph. The writer attends levees and grand audiences, and notes how the emperor's temper swings with his news. Before Italy he is condescending and agreeable, flushed by a Rochefort squadron's success and the Toulon fleet's escape from Nelson. After Milan he returns petulant, agitated, and rude.

A sad street scene shows the other side of empire, as an eighty year old beggar on the Quai de Voltaire wears a label confessing sixty thousand livres of rent lost. Soldiers give him coins, police seize him, and he vanishes. His name is De la Roche, once a chevalier, later a water carrier. Readers who like Napoleonic Paris will find vanity and ruin side by side.
3897-memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-be:
Lewis Goldsmith's sixth volume of Saint Cloud letters opens at a tea party given by a rich upstart. Once a scavenger, he is now legislator, commander of the Legion of Honor, and holder of eighteen millions of livres. There the writer meets Madame Chevalier, mistress and indirect cause of Paul the First's end. She is short, fat, and coarse, with a mouth large, eyes hollow, and language of the brothels. Prejudice aside, he finds her artful, vain, and disagreeable.

Police terror fills the later letters. An American vessel is seized at Bordeaux for English books that ill treat Bonaparte and his ministers. Its captain is kept in the Temple while cargo sells as lawful prize. A young German surgery student spends nine months in the same prison for a German printed book. Readers who like the empire's underside will find a book of spies, seizures, and fear.
3898-memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-be:
Lewis Goldsmith's seventh volume of Saint Cloud letters turns from Paris gossip to the diplomacy of empires. The cabinet of Saint Petersburg, loudly blamed by Saint Cloud, conducts itself with prudence without weakness and firmness without obstinacy. It refuses to endure impertinent innovations in court etiquette or in the emperor's language to legitimate sovereigns. The writer argues that spirited remonstrance from all princes might have moderated upstart vanity.

A portrait of Baron von Hardenberg follows, a minister whose life study was gaining information, kept through private agents paid for years across Europe. One agent met at Basle in 1796 strikes the writer as a poor choice. Readers who like diplomatic history will find a letter book of courts, spies, and wounded pride.
3899-memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-be:
This complete text gathers all of Lewis Goldsmith's Saint Cloud letters, the secret correspondence from Paris to London on Napoleon's court. The publisher's note promises particulars found in no other book, from a writer said to be Stewarton, friend of Josephine in her happier days. Lives of ministers and generals fill the letters. Royalist converts and risen soldiers appear beside anecdotes of Napoleon, Talleyrand, and Fouche, and notes on those who vanished after incurring displeasure.

A later passage praises a woman who loved her country and detested its tyrants. Never a worshipper of Bonaparte or a friend of Talleyrand, she was fit to have swayed with more glory than her husband had she held power. Sixteen girls of the Palais Royal demanding Holland passes from Fouche show the letters' range. Readers who want the whole Saint Cloud file will find a long and partisan chronicle.
4004-on-the-prospects-of-christianity-be:
Bernard Shaw's preface to Androcles and the Lion lays out his views on Christianity, the Gospels, and the life of Jesus. Shaw pictures Jesus taken before the high priest and then handed to Pilate, silent before accusers because he sees torment, death, and burial as a path to resurrection.

From that reading Shaw argues about faith, morals, and the church of his own day, in his usual bold, debating style. The preface stands apart from the play it fronts, as an essay in its own right. Readers who enjoy Shaw the thinker will find a long, provocative argument, while those who want only the play can skip ahead to it.
4201-literary-friends-and-acquaintance-a:
William Dean Howells's Literary Friends and Acquaintance looks back on a life among American writers. He recalls a letter from Lowell that turned defeat sweet and worthy, making misery bearable through a friend's benediction.

Love and gratitude, Howells notes, are often tongue-tied, while bitterness finds words all too easily. As often as he tried to tell Lowell of the letter's salvation, words failed him. The memoir suits readers who love literary history told personally, with friendships, not fame, at its center. Friendships, not fame, carry this literary memoir. Lowell, Hawthorne, and their circle pass through these pages.
4219-the-art-of-living-in-australia-toge:
A household guide to living in Australia pairs practical housekeeping with a long cookery section. A chapter on bedroom ventilation notes that few rented dwellings meet modern sanitary ideas, and that sleepers need fresh air through devices such as Tobin's ventilators.

The book moves from air, light, and rooms to food, health, and daily routine in a warm climate. Written for settlers and housekeepers, it favors plain advice over theory. Readers interested in Australian domestic life will find a useful, old-fashioned manual for home and table. Air, food, and routine get equal, practical attention.
4781-the-hohenzollerns-in-america-with-t:
Stephen Leacock wrote The Hohenzollerns in America, with The Bolsheviks in Berlin, and Other Impossibilities, as a book of comic impossibilities. Its contents run from The Hohenzollerns in America and With the Bolsheviks in Berlin, through Afternoon Tea with the Sultan, to Echoes of the War. That section includes The Boy Who Came Back, The War Sacrifices of Mr. Spugg, and If Germany Had Won, with war news, complaints, and side effects.

Other impossibilities include The Art of Conversation, Heroes and Heroines, The Discovery of America, and Fetching the Doctor. Leacock's preface proposes a proper punishment for the Hohenzollerns, Hapsburgs, Mecklenburgs, and Muckendorfs, and all such puppets and princelings. They should be made to work, not as generals, chiefs of staff, legislators, and land barons, but as plain labourers looking for work. Readers get Leacock's wartime satire, turning fallen royalty into ordinary workers.
4974-australia-twice-traversed-the-roman:
Ernest Giles's Australia Twice Traversed records two great journeys across the continent's interior, told in dated journal entries from August 1872 to 1876. Chapters march day by day: from August 4 to 30, 1872, then through September and October, into the long stretch to January 1873, and again through the second expedition's months.

Giles writes of water, desert, and endurance, with the romance of exploration in his title and hardship in his pages. The journal form keeps the reader beside the party, sharing its uncertainty about what lies beyond the next ridge. Readers get a firsthand record of Australian exploration at its most determined and most lonely.
538-jean-of-the-lazy-a:
B. M. Bower tells of Jean, a sixteen-year-old ranch girl on the Lazy A, in this western novel. One June day trouble blots out the ranch's peace. Jean, who scrubs floors and rides hard, must face a villain, a wounded name, and a film company that wants her as a leading lady. Lite, a cowhand, stands by her.

Bower writes with brisk, outdoor humor, mixing ranch work with movie plots and Los Angeles trips. Jean learns fear, pluck, and how to take matters into her own hands. The novel charms as a girl's western, where a range girl proves she can ride, act, and set things right.
5763-young-s-demonstrative-translation-o:
Young's Demonstrative Translation of Scientific Secrets, printed in Toronto in 1861, collects above five hundred useful receipts on a variety of subjects. Its parts give practical formulas in plain order, from a gallon of water with loaf sugar and tartaric acid to flour and egg whites beaten for a second receipt. The introduction states that the work's object is announced clearly in its title.

The book gives a Victorian household and workshop manual, where science means tested recipes rather than theory alone. Cooks, makers, and curious historians will find formulas for drinks, foods, and household arts, preserved with original spellings intact. The book offers a window into daily ingenuity in mid-nineteenth-century Canada, when a good receipt was valuable knowledge.
6611-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
The central states and Great Lakes fill Skinner's sixth volume, from an averted peril to the spell of Creve Coeur Lake. Saint Clair's obstinacy, a crime at Black Swamp, a house accursed, and Marquette's man-eater open a long, varied list. Lake Superior water gods, the witch of Pictured Rocks, and were-wolves of Detroit add a wilder note.

Hiawatha, an Indian messiah, and the vision of rescue bring Native lore to the fore, while river towns and falls ground the tales. Skinner keeps the pace brisk, moving from town to lake to wood. This volume gives the middle of America its own ghost map, full of water, woods, and old wrongs.
6669-godliness-being-reports-of-a-series:
Catherine Booth, of the Salvation Army, speaks on godliness in a series of addresses given at St. James's Hall, London, during 1881. Daniel Steele's introduction presents her main doctrines with force, and the publishers call the book a favor to lovers of Christianity in earnest. An earlier work, Aggressive Christianity, had already won wide favor.

Booth's talks urge a faith that shows in daily life, not just in words, with warmth and plain power. The reports keep her voice close, as if heard in the hall. Godliness is a direct, earnest book of Victorian preaching, valuable to readers of revival history and of women's preaching.
6707-st-patrick-s-day-or-the-scheming-li:
Richard Brinsley Sheridan's farce, first acted at Covent Garden in 1775, opens in Lieutenant O'Connor's lodgings in an English town. Soldiers crowd in, arguing in platoons: each man wants to speak at once, that they may be heard the better, while the corporal, the lieutenant's countryman, seeks to lead them. The joke lands at once.

A scheming lieutenant, a credulous justice, a doctor named Rosy, and two lively women drive the short, brisk plot. The farce is all talk, trick, and Irish wit, played for laughs. St. Patrick's Day is a bright, small Sheridan comedy, easy to read and still funny on the page.
6894-chimes-of-mission-bells-an-historic:
Maria Antonia Field sketches California and her missions, dedicating the book to Junipero Serra and to her great grandparents Esteban and Catalina Munras. She thanks her mother, who set the hymns of the mission fathers in modern notation, and her parish priest, who opened the early archives of San Carlos Mission and Monterey. Andrew Dickson White's Fiat Money Inflation in France tells how revolutionary France printed paper money, what it brought, and how it ended. White, former president of Cornell and former minister to Russia and ambassador to Germany, built the book on a collection of revolutionary documents gathered in France before the American Civil War.
